# Generated by bench/stages.py from models/web_service/model.yaml.
# The finished model with everything the book has not introduced by the end
# of ch03 removed, so that a reader can see it at 11 nodes. Not a model
# anybody would ship. Do not edit: say which chapter introduces a node in
# build-order.yaml instead.
dsl: 2
model: web_service_provenance
title: >-
  A web service and its data, on a fleet of Linux hosts — The
  first number somebody else supplied
currency: USD
description: The web service model as it stands at the end of ch03.
nodes:
  peak_request_rate_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate, day one
    value: 8000
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The service owners estimate the request rate in the busy
        hour. They have a spread of plausible rates in mind and
        round it to one number; ch04 replaces it with the spread.
    range: [500, 40000]
  stored_data_t0:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: TB
    value: 15
    label: records held, day one
    note: >-
      This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how
      much you hold today. Nobody can count next quarter's busy
      hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they
      grow, and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the
      level alike.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The service owners estimate what the service holds today:
        its database and the objects users have uploaded, before
        replication, indexes or compression. It has not been counted
        yet, and counting it would turn the estimate into a fact.
    range: [1, 200]
  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: annual growth factor
    value: 1.3
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        Not measured. The service owners estimate how fast demand
        grows each year. One number cannot say how sure they are
        of it, so ch04 replaces it with a spread.
    range: [1.0, 2.0]
  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: the refresh cycle this fleet is bought against
    range: [3, 8]
  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    label: one year
    note: >-
      The model multiplies demand by `annual_growth ** horizon_periods`.
      Because `annual_growth` is applied once per year, the exponent
      must count years, not a length of time. Dividing the horizon
      by `one_year` produces that count. Appendix D has the rest
      of the conversions that bite.
    provenance:
      kind: fact
      source: definition
  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year
  peak_request_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: request/second
    label: peak request rate at horizon
    formula: peak_request_rate_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods
  stored_data:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: records held at horizon
    formula: stored_data_t0 * annual_growth ** horizon_periods
  ram_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: GiB/host
    value: 64
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: >-
        spec sheet: the modules fitted. The sheet says 64 GB and
        means GiB — appendix D — and the operating system will
        report less than either, which is os_reserve's job
    range: [8, 1024]
  os_reserve:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.1
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The share of memory the kernel, the agents and the page
        cache floor keep before the service sees any. One number
        for now: it differs from host to host and has not been
        measured on these hosts, so ch04 replaces it with a spread.
    range: [0.0, 0.4]
  ram_for_service:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB/host
    label: memory the service can use, per host
    note: >-
      Gibibytes in, decimal terabytes out — the build converts
      (appendix D). Declared in the unit the working set is counted
      in, so that the chain which divides one by the other rounds
      a count of hosts and not a count of hosts times nine hundred
      and thirty-one.
    formula: ram_per_host * (1 - os_reserve)
outputs: [peak_request_rate, stored_data, ram_for_service]
correlations: []
